section.title: The Sign against Egypt and Cush
section.sectionRationale: This brief narrative interrupts the oracles against the nations, chapters 13 to 23, with a living parable: for three years Isaiah himself walks naked and barefoot as a prophetic sign, dramatizing in his own body the shame that will come on Egypt and Cush, the very powers Judah was tempted to trust for rescue from Assyria.
section.thesis: Isaiah's own humiliating sign act, three years walking naked and barefoot, dramatizes the coming shame of Egypt and Cush before Assyria, warning Judah that the nations she hopes in for deliverance cannot even save themselves.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the historical setting of Sargon's commander capturing Ashdod; the LORD's command that Isaiah act out the sign in his own body; and the sign's fulfillment as Assyria leads Egypt and Cush away naked and ashamed.

verses.text: Before the year that the chief commander, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and attacked and captured it,

units.label: Isaiah's sign in his own body
units.note: naked and barefoot for three years

verses.text: the LORD had already spoken through Isaiah son of Amoz, saying, “Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet.” And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot.
Then the LORD said, “Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a {{owth|sign}} and {{mopheth|omen}} against Egypt and Cush,

units.label: The sign fulfilled: Egypt and Cush led away in shame

verses.text: so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with bared buttocks, to Egypt's shame.
Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed.

And on that day the dwellers of this coastland will say, ‘See what has happened to our source of hope, those to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?’”

owth.gloss: A sign, a visible token that points beyond itself to a truth or coming event. God frequently gives signs to confirm His word, but here the sign is Isaiah's own body and humiliation, making the prophet himself a living, walking sermon.

mopheth.gloss: A wonder, portent, or omen, often paired with owth, sign, to describe an act or event that startles observers into recognizing God's hand at work. Isaiah's three years of nakedness functioned as exactly this kind of arresting, unforgettable portent.

basic.context: For three years, Isaiah obeyed a shocking command: to walk around naked and barefoot as a living object lesson. This was not madness but prophetic theater, dramatizing what would soon happen to Egypt and Cush, the very nations Judah's leaders wanted to trust for help against Assyria. When Assyria's army did come, it would strip and lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives in the same shameful state Isaiah had already displayed.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical episode, tied to the actual Assyrian capture of Ashdod around 711 BC under Sargon II, and it functions as a warning against a real, contemporary temptation: relying on Egypt and Cush rather than the LORD. It is not a call for believers today to imitate Isaiah's exact actions, but it does model how God sometimes uses costly, embodied obedience to make an unmistakable point.
basic.originalLanguages: Isaiah's ordeal is called both an owth, sign, and a mopheth, omen or wonder, the pairing Scripture often uses for acts too striking to ignore. His humiliation was designed to be remembered and to strip away, in advance, any illusions Judah had about the safety of trusting Egypt and Cush.
basic.typology: Isaiah's willing embrace of shame and exposure as a sign for others' sake foreshadows Christ, who was stripped, mocked, and shamed publicly, not for His own sin but so that His humiliation would become the sign and wonder that saves those who trust in Him rather than in false securities.
basic.christ: Isaiah bore shame in his own body as a sign to warn others away from false hope; Christ bore far greater shame, stripped and exposed on the cross, not merely as a warning but as the actual payment for sin, so that all who look to Him rather than to any earthly power are saved rather than put to shame, Romans 10:11.
basic.god: God is willing to use costly, even humiliating obedience from His servants to make His warnings vivid and unforgettable. He is also relentlessly opposed to His people's false hopes; no earthly power, however impressive, can shelter those who trust it instead of Him.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 30:1-5 warn similarly against trusting Egypt rather than the LORD. Hebrews 12:2 speaks of Christ enduring the cross, scorning its shame, echoing this pattern of costly obedience for others' sake. Romans 10:11 promises that none who trust in Him will be put to shame.
basic.oneStory: Isaiah's three years of humiliation warn that every hope but the LORD ends in shame, since even Egypt and Cush cannot save themselves, let alone anyone who trusts in them. This anticipates Christ, who bore the ultimate shame on the cross so that everyone who trusts in Him, rather than in any earthly power, will never be put to shame.

context.literary:
The chapter has the clean shape of a prophetic sign act: a time note, a command, the prophet's obedience, an interpretation, and the effect on those who see it. Verse 1 fixes the occasion. Verse 2 gives the command and the obedience in one breath, 'And Isaiah did so.' Verses 3 and 4 spell out the meaning, and verses 5 and 6 report the shock of those who watch. Nothing is left to be guessed, and that is itself a sign of how pointed the lesson was.

The chapter is also a seam in the book. It is the only place in Isaiah 13 to 23 where the prophet is described in the third person, and it gathers up the two oracles before it. 'Egypt and Cush' is the pairing here, so chapter 20 joins the unnamed ambassadors of Cush in chapter 18 and the Egypt of chapter 19 in a single verdict. The oracle against the nations, which has been running in cycles, receives its hard, practical conclusion: do not put your hope in either of them.

Three details deserve notice. First, the LORD calls Isaiah 'My servant,' verse 3, a title given to him nowhere else, and it is the title the book will later give to the figure who bears shame for others, Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13. Second, the vocabulary of looking is central again. What Egypt and Cush were to Judah is described in verse 5 with a word from the verb to look, so they were the thing Judah's eyes were fixed on, which takes the reader back to the question of where to look in chapters 17 and 18. Third, the chapter ends with a question and no answer. 'How then can we escape?' The answer is held for the rest of the book, in the stone laid in Zion, Isaiah 28:16, and in the 'repentance and rest' of Isaiah 30:15, and in the deliverance of Jerusalem, Isaiah 37.
context.historical:
Verse 1 is the most precisely dated notice in this part of the book. In 711 BC the chief commander of Sargon II of Assyria captured Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities. Sargon is named in the Bible only here. The title 'chief commander,' tartan in Hebrew, was an Assyrian office for the commander of the army, and the same title turns up when Sennacherib's officers come to Jerusalem, 2 Kings 18:17. Assyrian records speak of a revolt at Ashdod and of a ruler who fled south when the city fell, and they report that he was eventually handed over to Assyria. Such details fit the situation Isaiah describes, in which Philistia and her neighbours had looked to Egypt and Cush for help.

The command came before the city fell and the sign ran for three years. In an ancient city the sight of the prophet naked and barefoot would have been a daily provocation. Sackcloth was the garb of mourning, and Jacob put it around his waist when he grieved for Joseph, Genesis 37:34. Isaiah is told to remove it. We cannot be sure whether it was an everyday prophet's garment or a mourner's covering, but its removal left him in the state in which captives were led away, and that is the point of the sign.

The effects of the prophecy were seen within the following half century. Assyrian kings invaded Egypt in 671 BC, when Esarhaddon took Memphis, and again in the 660s, when Ashurbanipal reached Thebes, an event that Nahum 3:8-10 recalls with the line that Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength and yet she went into captivity. Judah, under Hezekiah, would hear the same argument from an Assyrian officer in 701 BC, who called Egypt a 'splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it,' 2 Kings 18:21 and the officer's words echo what Isaiah had acted out years before.

The sign was given at a moment when Judah's leaders were tempted by envoys and treaties, and it is the answer to their question whether Egypt and Cush could be relied on.
context.canonical:
Isaiah's sign action belongs with a group of prophetic enactments in which the prophet's own body or life becomes the message. Isaiah himself declared that he and his children were 'signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts,' Isaiah 8:18. Hosea's marriage, Jeremiah's yoke, Ezekiel's packed bags and his siege model all belong to this tradition, and Micah says of himself, 'I will walk barefoot and naked,' Micah 1:8. In Ezekiel 12:1-7 the prophet leaves by the wall of his own house like an exile 'as they watch,' so that the people will see the lesson played out in front of them.

The theme of trusting Egypt runs through Isaiah's own book. Isaiah 30:1-5 warns that Pharaoh's protection will 'become your shame,' and Isaiah 31:1-3 says that the Egyptians 'are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit.' The Assyrian officer's insult in Isaiah 36:6 and 2 Kings 18:21 presents Egypt as a splintered reed. Psalm 20:7 and Jeremiah 17:5-8 state the principle in general form: cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD.

The language of shame leads forward to the Servant of the LORD. In Isaiah 50:6-7 the Servant offers His back to those who strike Him and does not hide His face from scorn, saying that He will 'not be put to shame.' Isaiah 49:23 promises that those who hope in the LORD 'will never be put to shame,' and Isaiah 25:8 says that God will 'remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth.'

The New Testament takes up both strands. Paul quotes the promise that 'anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame,' Romans 10:11. The writer to the Hebrews takes Isaiah 8:18 for Christ, 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me,' Hebrews 2:13, and speaks of Jesus who 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2, and who suffered outside the city gate, so that we may go to Him 'bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:12-13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
This chapter was meant to be remembered. A message spoken once can be argued with, but a prophet who walks through the streets stripped for three years cannot easily be ignored, and Isaiah's purpose was to leave Jerusalem unable to say it had not been told. The immediate audience was the circle of officials and advisers who were weighing a pact with Egypt and Cush, and the sign says to them in the plainest possible language that the powers they are eyeing will themselves be paraded as prisoners.

He also meant to clarify what faith is. The sign takes the question out of the realm of strategy and puts it in the realm of trust. Isaiah is not asking Judah to prefer Assyria, or to guess which empire will win. He is asking them to stop treating any human power as a refuge, because every one of them will be exposed. The unanswered question of verse 6, 'How then can we escape?', is the question that the rest of the book answers with the LORD Himself.

Finally, it tells Isaiah's readers something about the cost of speaking for God. The prophet is not a distant commentator but a man who shares in the humiliation he announces. The chapter calls the first hearers, and the later readers of the book, to take seriously a word that was spoken at that price.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a command given to one prophet at one time. It is not a pattern that believers are meant to copy, and nothing in the New Testament suggests that obedience to God requires public nakedness. To read the passage as a warrant for shocking acts in the name of prophecy would be a serious mistake, and to dismiss it as bizarre would be another, because it shows what a costly obedience can look like.

What the passage prescribes is the conclusion it draws: whatever we are tempted to treat as our rescue besides the LORD will end in shame, and the right response is trust in Him, as Psalm 20:7 puts it, 'Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.' It also invites a posture toward obedience: a servant of God may be asked to bear reproach so that others may understand. Paul's language of being fools for Christ and the Hebrews call to go out to Jesus 'outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:13, are the New Testament forms of the same willingness.

debates.question: Was Isaiah completely naked, and for how long?

views.label: Fully naked for a full three years
views.case: The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for naked, and verse 4 speaks of the exposed bodies of the captives, so the sign matched the humiliation it announced. A literal three year period fits the phrase 'for three years' in verse 3.

views.label: Stripped of outer clothing, in a tunic or loincloth
views.case: The same Hebrew word can describe someone stripped of an outer garment. Saul 'stripped off his robes' and 'lay naked,' 1 Samuel 19:24, and Peter, who had removed his outer garment, is called naked in John 21:7. On this reading Isaiah took off the sackcloth and sandals but was not stripped bare, which would have been less offensive in the society he was addressing.

views.label: The three years describe the sign, not a continuous act
views.case: The Hebrew order of the phrase can attach 'three years' to the sign and omen, so that the sign pointed to a three year period, as in Isaiah 16:14, rather than lasting three years in a row. On this view Isaiah may have acted the part in the public square at intervals.

debates.bearing: The text itself does not decide, and the teaching does not depend on it. In every reading the prophet was exposed to ridicule in a manner that matched what the captives would endure. The key is not how much he wore but that his body became the message.

debates.question: Who speaks in verse 6, the people of the coast or Judah?

views.label: The people of the Philistine coast
views.case: Ashdod had just fallen, and the coastal cities had sought help from Egypt and Cush. The phrase 'this coastland' fits the Philistine seaboard well, and their cry would be that the powers they trusted have failed.

views.label: Judah, looking at the fall of Ashdod
views.case: The phrase 'to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria' fits Judah's own posture, and the chapter is addressed to Judah's leaders. On this reading the speaker is a Judean who sees what has happened to the hope of the region and recognises his own danger.

views.label: The coastlands in a wider sense
views.case: The word translated coastland is used elsewhere in Isaiah for distant lands, and some read it as all the peoples of the Mediterranean who watch the fall of Egypt and Cush and ask how they can escape.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity is useful. The question is addressed to whoever trusted the same hope. Judah would be tempted to say it of itself, and the book keeps asking it until the answer is given.

study.originalLanguages:
The two Hebrew words the chapter uses for Isaiah's condition are arom, naked, and yachef, barefoot. Barefoot is the sign of grief and humiliation, as when David went up the Mount of Olives 'weeping as he went up. His head was covered, and he was walking barefoot,' 2 Samuel 15:30. The word for naked can mean fully unclothed or stripped of outer garments, as 1 Samuel 19:24 and John 21:7 show for Saul and for Peter, and this is one reason why interpreters differ about how far the sign went. Verse 4 speaks of the captives with 'bared buttocks,' and the word for buttocks, shet, appears in the shaming of David's envoys, when Hanun cut their garments off, 2 Samuel 10:4, where the BSB renders it 'hips.' The common thread is shame inflicted on the body.

The pair 'sign and omen,' the lexicon's owth and mopheth, has a particular history. 'Signs and wonders' is the stock phrase of the exodus, where the LORD says, 'I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,' Exodus 7:3. By using the same vocabulary of Isaiah's body, the text turns the exodus language around. Egypt had been the stage on which God worked signs against Pharaoh, and now a prophet in Judah is the sign against Egypt. Isaiah 8:18 uses the same pairing of his family: 'signs and symbols in Israel.'

Verse 3 calls Isaiah 'My servant,' using the word 'ebed. The title belongs to Moses, David and the prophets, as in Amos 3:7, and it is the same word that the book later uses of the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13. It is not a reason to equate Isaiah with that Servant, but it places the prophet's shame in the neighbourhood of the Servant's, a point Christians will see fulfilled.

In verse 5 Cush is 'their hope,' and the Hebrew word, mabbat, is built on the verb nabat, to look. Cush is literally the thing they looked to. That sets the chapter beside Isaiah 22:11, 'you did not look to the One who made it,' and beside the promise in Isaiah 17:7 that men will look to their Maker. Egypt is 'their boast,' tiferet, a word for splendor or glory. In Isaiah 46:13 the LORD promises to 'adorn Israel with My splendor,' using the same word. Judah's real glory was always to be what God gave them, not what Egypt offered. The two verbs of the verse, 'dismayed and ashamed,' use the word for shame that recurs when God promises that those who hope in Him 'will never be put to shame,' Isaiah 49:23.

The final question, 'How then can we escape?', uses a verb for escaping from danger that the Old Testament often uses of the survivors of a disaster. The prophet leaves it hanging so that the reader supplies the answer that the book gives later: the refuge is the LORD, and those who trust Him will not be put to shame.

typology.type: The prophet's body as the sign, Isaiah 20:2-3
typology.fulfillment: God makes His servant's own person the message. The pattern reaches its fullest form in Christ. Simeon says the Child is 'appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,' Luke 2:34, and Hebrews applies Isaiah 8:18 to Him, 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me,' Hebrews 2:13. The escalation is that Isaiah was a sign pointing to a coming judgment, while Christ is the sign of God's salvation and is Himself what the sign points to. The type falls short because Isaiah bore humiliation for a time and for a warning, whereas Christ bore it to remove the cause.

Egypt and Cush were to be led away exposed, to the shame of those who trusted them. Jesus, though innocent, was stripped by the soldiers, who put a scarlet robe on Him and later divided His clothing, Matthew 27:28 and John 19:23-24, fulfilling Psalm 22:18. The correspondence is of the outward form of the shame. The escalation lies in the cause: the captives were exposed for their own failure and for the failure of the powers that could not save them, while Jesus was exposed in the place of others. The type falls short because the shame of Egypt was a judgment and the shame of Christ was a bearing of judgment on behalf of the guilty.

typology.type: Shame carried outside the camp, Isaiah 20:3-4
typology.fulfillment: The prophet carries a disgrace that is not his own so that others may see and turn. Hebrews says that Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' and calls us to go to Him 'outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:12-13. In Christ the pattern becomes substitution and not only witness. He scorned the shame, Hebrews 12:2, and because He did, those who hope in Him 'will never be put to shame,' Romans 10:11. The type falls short because Isaiah's sign could warn but not cleanse.

typology.type: Nakedness and the covering of shame, Isaiah 20:2-4
typology.fulfillment: Nakedness in Scripture first appears without shame, Genesis 2:25, and then with it, Genesis 3:7, and the Bible's story is partly the story of how God deals with exposure. Isaiah's sign shows the shame of a people who have nothing to cover them. In Christ the covering is supplied. Believers 'have clothed yourselves with Christ,' Galatians 3:27, and the Lord counsels the church to buy 'white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed,' Revelation 3:18. Isaiah 61:10 rejoices that God has 'clothed me with garments of salvation.' The type falls short because Isaiah's exposure only announced shame, while Christ's clothing takes it away.

study.christ:
Isaiah 20 leads to Christ first by the figure of the servant who carries shame in his own body. God calls Isaiah 'My servant,' and the humiliation he bears is a message to others. That pattern belongs to the Servant of the LORD in the later chapters of the book, who says, 'I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle,' Isaiah 50:6, and who adds, 'I know that I will not be put to shame,' Isaiah 50:7. Isaiah the prophet is a shadow of this Servant, and the shadow has real contours: he is obedient, he is exposed, and he is exposed for the sake of others.

It leads to Christ by contrast, because the contrast shows what is new. Isaiah went barefoot and naked as a warning of what others would suffer. Christ was stripped and mocked, Matthew 27:28 and Mark 15:17-20, and His garments were divided by lots, John 19:23-24, but not as a sign pointing to someone else's fate. He bore it as His own, in the place of the guilty. Paul puts it starkly: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The writer to the Hebrews says He 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2. Isaiah's sign could only say that shame was coming. Christ takes it.

It leads to Christ by the central claim of the chapter, that every refuge but the LORD will fail. Egypt and Cush were people's hope, and they could not save themselves. Christ is the one whose name never fails those who trust in Him. 'Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame,' Romans 10:11, and Isaiah 49:23 had promised that 'those who hope in Me will never be put to shame.' The promise is as old as the prophets and is fulfilled in the person who was put to shame in their place.

And it leads to Christ by reversal. Isaiah 25:8 says that God will swallow up death and 'remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth.' The resurrection is the beginning of that removal, and the clothing of the redeemed in white is its completion, Revelation 3:18. The chapter that ends with shame and an unanswered question is thus answered in the One who suffered shame and then rose.

We should stay with what the text allows. Isaiah is not simply Christ, and the details of Ashdod and Sargon are not codes. The link is the pattern of the servant who bears shame and the claim that trust in the LORD alone does not end in disgrace.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter says about God is that He speaks before events happen. The word to Isaiah comes before Ashdod falls, and the sign goes on for three years before its meaning is fulfilled. God does not simply act in history; He tells His servants what He is about to do, so that when it comes it will be known as His doing. The date at the opening of the chapter is therefore a statement about His foreknowledge and His patience.

He is a God who wants His people to understand. A sign like this takes time and costs a great deal, and the cost is God's way of making sure the message gets through. The prophet is not an instrument without a will. He is called 'My servant,' a title of affection and dignity, and God shares the weight of the message with him. This tells us that God is willing to ask a great deal of His servants for the sake of others, and that He honors them even while He asks.

He is a God who opposes false hope with a firm hand. The chapter does not simply say that Egypt and Cush are unreliable. It says that those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed. This is a revelation of God's jealousy for trust. He is not threatened by empires, but He will not let His people hand to an empire the confidence that belongs to Him. Elsewhere He says through Isaiah, 'Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils,' Isaiah 2:22.

He is a God who rules the powers that look most secure. The Assyrian commander, the fall of Ashdod, the captives from Egypt and Cush, are all part of a plan He knows in advance. The nations are moved about by forces that think of themselves as free, and the book of Isaiah insists that behind them is a hand that is not frightened. At the same time the chapter does not make God a tyrant. The question in verse 6 is left open, and the invitation of the book is that the refuge is available in Him.

He is also the God who identifies with those who are shamed. In this chapter He allows His own servant to be shamed to get His message across, and in the fullness of time He sends His Son to be shamed in the place of the guilty. The God of Isaiah 20 is not distant from disgrace. He steps into it.

For worship, this means that we are invited to bring our fears of insecurity to the one place they can be answered. We confess the false hopes we have held, whether political, financial or personal, and we ask for the courage to follow the God who is worth trusting even when His commands are costly. And we thank Him that the shame we deserve was carried by another.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah says that he and his children are 'signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts.' Chapter 20 is the most extreme case of the same self-understanding, in which the prophet's own life is the message, and Hebrews 2:13 takes the verse to Christ.

Judah's envoys travel to Zoan and Hanes to seek Egypt's protection, and the LORD says it will 'become your shame.' The chapter is the spoken counterpart to the sign of chapter 20, and the same shame language links them.

The woe against those who go down to Egypt for help and 'do not look to the Holy One of Israel,' with the line that Egyptians 'are men, not God.' It states in words the lesson that chapter 20 shows in a body, and it uses the same language of looking.

Sennacherib's officer stands at the aqueduct and mocks Hezekiah's reliance on Egypt as a 'splintered reed of a staff.' The Assyrian's words, though meant to demoralise, echo what Isaiah's sign had said years before.

Ezekiel packs his bags and leaves through a hole in the wall in front of the people, to be a sign to the rebellious house. The sign act is the same genre as Isaiah's, with the same purpose: the message is played out so they can no longer say they did not see.

Micah says of himself, 'I will walk barefoot and naked,' as an act of lament over the coming judgment. It is the nearest parallel to Isaiah's sign and shows that the prophets sometimes embodied the grief of the message in public view.

The Servant offers His back to those who strike Him and does not hide His face from scorn, and says He will not be put to shame. It is the later chapter in which the prophet's shame is carried to its fullest, and it gives the theological ground for the Servant who bears disgrace.
God promises that those who hope in Him 'will never be put to shame.' It is the direct answer to the shame of those who hoped in Cush and Egypt in 20:5, and it uses the same word for shame.

Paul takes the promise that no one who believes will be put to shame and applies it to everyone who trusts in Christ, Jew or Greek. It is the New Testament answer to the question of verse 6, because the refuge that does not fail is Christ.

Jesus 'endured the cross, scorning its shame.' Isaiah bore humiliation as a sign, and Jesus bore it as a rescue, and the writer calls readers to fix their eyes on Him. The contrast illuminates what Isaiah's sign could not do.

Jesus suffered outside the gate, and believers are to go to Him 'outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.' It carries the sign of Isaiah into the life of the church, where shame for the sake of the gospel is a share in Christ's.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 20 sits in the part of the Bible's story where God's people are tempted, again and again, to find their safety somewhere other than in Him. The temptation is as old as the fall. In Genesis 3 the man and the woman, exposed and ashamed, sewed leaves together for themselves, and the whole of the Bible is the story of what God does about human attempts at self-covering. Isaiah's generation tries a different covering, a treaty with Egypt and Cush, and the prophet's body in the street is God's answer: no such covering will last.

The chapter answers a question left from earlier in the book, where Isaiah told Ahaz in chapter 7 to stand firm in faith, and Ahaz would not. Hezekiah now faces the same test with different empires, and the sign of chapter 20 is part of the instruction the later king will either heed or ignore. The story of Hezekiah in chapters 36 and 37 shows what it looks like when the instruction is finally taken: he prays, the LORD answers, and the army that has mocked trust in Egypt is turned back.

The chapter also sets up the Servant. Isaiah's shame is a shadow, and in chapters 49 to 53 the shadow takes shape, as the Servant offers His back and does not hide His face. In the Gospels the shadow becomes flesh. Jesus is stripped, mocked and crucified outside the city, and by bearing the shame He opens the way for those who trust in Him to be freed from it. Paul reads the Old Testament promise of no shame as fulfilled in Him, Romans 10:11.

The story ends with the shame removed. 'He will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:8, and God will 'remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth.' In the new creation the redeemed are clothed in white, and the shameful nakedness that began in Genesis 3 is covered for good, Revelation 3:18. The false hopes of Egypt and Cush give way to the one hope that does not fail, and the question of Isaiah 20:6 receives its answer: there is an escape, and it is the Lord.

quiz.q: What did the LORD command Isaiah to do as a prophetic sign?

options.text: Walk around naked and barefoot for three years.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 state this command and its three-year duration explicitly.

options.text: Build a model of the Assyrian army out of clay.
options.note: Not found in this text; the sign was Isaiah's own body and state, not a model.
This is a different kind of sign found elsewhere in Scripture, not commanded here.

options.text: Wear sackcloth continuously for three years.
options.note: Close, since sackcloth is mentioned, but the command was specifically to remove it, not to wear it.

quiz.q: What was Isaiah's sign meant to warn against?

options.text: Trusting Egypt and Cush for deliverance from Assyria.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6 explicitly name this false hope as the sign's target.
Not the subject of this passage; the concern is political trust in Egypt and Cush.

options.text: Trusting in Judah's own military strength.
options.note: Related in spirit to misplaced trust, but the specific warning names Egypt and Cush as the false hope, not Judah's own army.

quiz.q: What actually happened to Egypt and Cush according to the sign's fulfillment?

options.text: Assyria led their captives away naked and barefoot, in humiliating shame.
options.note: Verse 4 describes exactly this outcome, matching Isaiah's own embodied sign.

options.text: They successfully repelled the Assyrian army.
options.note: The opposite; they are led away in defeat and shame.

options.text: They formed a permanent alliance with Assyria.
options.note: Not described in this passage; they are conquered, not allied.

options.text: They were spared entirely due to their wealth.
options.note: The text describes their humiliation, not exemption from judgment.

quiz.q: How does Isaiah's costly sign act point forward to Christ?

options.text: It foreshadows Christ, who bore real shame and humiliation at the cross for others' salvation.
options.note: Hebrews 12:2 speaks of Christ enduring the cross and scorning its shame, echoing this pattern.

options.text: It shows that Jesus never experienced any suffering or shame.
options.note: The opposite is true; Christ's suffering and shame at the cross are central to the gospel.

options.text: It proves that prophets today must perform similar acts.
options.note: The passage describes a specific historical command, not a universal pattern for believers to imitate literally.

options.text: It is unrelated to any New Testament theme.
options.note: There is a real typological connection to Christ's shame and humiliation, even though the passage's primary meaning is historical warning.

questions: Isaiah endured three years of public humiliation out of obedience to God's word. What costly obedience is God asking of you that feels humiliating or hard to explain to others?
Judah was tempted to trust Egypt and Cush rather than the LORD for deliverance. What powerful ally or resource are you tempted to trust instead of God right now?
The very nations Judah hoped in were themselves led away in shame. Where have you placed hope in something that, in the end, could not even save itself?
Isaiah's shame in his own body previews the far greater shame Christ bore at the cross. How does knowing Christ bore shame for you change how you carry your own moments of shame or humiliation?
The coastland dwellers asked in despair, how then can we escape? Where do you need to remember that escape and rescue are found in the LORD alone, not in any earthly power?

translationNotes.note: Naked most likely describes Isaiah stripped of his outer garment of sackcloth, though the term can denote complete nakedness; either reading preserves the intended public shame and humiliation of the sign.
The chief commander renders a Hebrew military title, Tartan, an Assyrian office rather than a personal name, referring to Sargon II's field commander who besieged and captured Ashdod.
